title: Nothing outside

cards: You're stuck in traffic. Not moving. You're going to be late, and there's nothing you can do.
The jaw sets, the fingers drum, and a voice in your head starts narrating how unfair this is, as if the traffic were happening outside the world, a glitch in how things are supposed to go.
Most frustration has that shape: this shouldn't be happening. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven has a single word it repeats, line after line, that answers the feeling. The word is hukam.

teach.b: Hukam is the divine order, the command, the way God's will runs through everything. You met it last year in Japji.
Yesterday's pictures, the earth held up with no support, things born and merging back, high and low, every color and form, all ride on one word, opening line after line: hukme, by the order.

teach.h: NO ONE IS OUTSIDE THE HUKAM.
teach.b: Guru Nanak said it plainly in Japji: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside the hukam. Now the traffic jam.
Frustration says: this is outside how things should be. Hukam says: there is no outside. The jam is inside the order.
So is the meeting you'll be late for. So is your frustration. That doesn't make it pleasant.

And it doesn't mean God personally put a truck in your lane to teach you a lesson; Sikh teachers don't usually read hukam as that kind of puzzle. It means the frustrating thing isn't a glitch in the universe.
It's part of the same order that holds the earth up.

When nothing is outside, there's nothing left to fight the way frustration wants to fight. Japji also says that whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. The ego is the part that insists things go its way.

how: Sikhs understand hukam, the divine order, as encompassing everything, as Japji puts it, and many recall it in frustration or hardship as a way of loosening the ego's demand that things go its way.

o: the outside world doesn't matter, only the inner
all things, even frustrations, lie within God's order
leave your troubles at the door, not in your heart

p: no more saying I, I, I

s: hukam means God arranges each annoyance to teach you a lesson
Sikh teachers don't usually read hukam that way; it's the order everything is inside.
Japji says no one is outside the hukam
everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside it.
in the stanza, birth and merging back both happen by the order

games.q: you're stuck in traffic, late, and fuming that this shouldn't be happening. what does hukam say?
o: you're right: it's a glitch in the universe.
there's no outside: the jam, and your frustration, are inside the order.
someone up there is punishing you.
games.why: hukmai andar sabh ko: everything is inside the order, and that quietly loosens the ego's fight.

practice: Bring up something small that annoyed you today, a slow line, a rude message, a broken thing, and feel where it lives in you.
Breathing in, say silently: this too is inside; breathing out: nothing outside; and let the feeling stay, held in the same order as everything else, until its edge softens even a little.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Nothing outside. Everything is within the hukam, the divine order, even what frustrates us; no one and nothing is outside it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: hukam, the divine order or command; 'hukme', by the order, drums through ashtpadi eleven's first stanza.

carryVoice: Your line: this too is inside. Even the traffic, even the frustration. Day four hundred eighty, done.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)

sources.ref: Japji Sahib, pauri 2 (Ang 1): everyone within the hukam, none outside
